subject: root-vs-trust-list-dispute
notes: The dispute between a single no-PII certification root (Position A) and plural, overlapping trust lists (Position B) is largely a misunderstanding over what "central authority" means: each side's objection targets a real, specific weakness of the other — A is exposed to root compromise, operator coercion, and unappealable exclusion; B to Sybil/synthetic identities and relying parties being unable to judge unfamiliar credentials — and a hybrid architecture (plural roots that relying parties choose among, one shared assurance-level vocabulary, append-only transparency logs for admission/issuance/revocation, PII held by the person or community with pairwise pseudonyms, and credential portability) satisfies both sides' core requirements, leaving as genuine residual cruxes only (1) whether enrollment/proofing data is pooled anywhere, (2) whether a large high-assurance root is acceptable when it is not exclusive, and (3) who governs the shared assurance vocabulary and log format.

subject: position-a-objections
notes: Position A's objections to plural trust lists identify genuine failure modes: without a single root, Sybil/synthetic identities can be minted by any admitted issuer, and relying parties lacking a shared frame cannot evaluate credentials from unfamiliar issuers.

subject: position-b-objections
notes: Position B's objections to a single certification root identify genuine failure modes: a single root is a single point of compromise, its operator is a single point of legal/political coercion, and exclusion decisions by a sole root have no alternative path of appeal.

subject: central-authority
notes: The two sides use "central authority" to mean different things: A means a shared reference frame (common assurance vocabulary, auditable admission), while B hears an exclusive gatekeeper (one operator who can deny participation). Much of the disagreement is therefore terminological rather than substantive.

subject: hybrid-architecture
notes: A hybrid of plural relying-party-chosen roots, one shared assurance-level vocabulary, append-only transparency logs for admission/issuance/revocation, PII held locally with pairwise pseudonyms, and credential portability addresses each named weakness: plural roots + portability answer compromise, coercion and exclusion; shared vocabulary + logs answer unfamiliar-credential evaluation and give Sybil resistance a verifiable basis.

subject: residual-cruxes
notes: After the hybrid is adopted, what remains genuinely contested is: (1) whether enrollment/proofing data is pooled anywhere (a privacy vs. Sybil-resistance trade-off the architecture does not dissolve), (2) whether a large high-assurance root is acceptable when non-exclusive (a question about de facto vs. de jure centralization), and (3) who governs the shared vocabulary and log format (the hybrid reintroduces a thin coordination point).

subject: core-requirements
notes: Assumption: the "core requirements" attributed to each side (A: Sybil resistance and legibility of credentials; B: no single point of compromise, coercion, or exclusion) are actually what partisans of each position would endorse as their non-negotiables, rather than a reconstruction convenient to the hybrid.

subject: relying-parties
notes: Assumption: relying parties have the capacity and incentive to actually select among roots, rather than defaulting to a bundled list set by a platform or vendor, which would recreate de facto single-root dynamics.

subject: pairwise-pseudonyms
notes: Assumption: holding PII locally and presenting pairwise pseudonyms does not undermine the uniqueness guarantees Sybil resistance needs; i.e., one-person-one-credential can be enforced at the issuer without cross-relying-party linkability. If this fails, crux (1) is not residual but central.
